problem_statement.title: Questions that are hidden by default
problem_statement.body:
### Actual Situation

Our org has one big template that is used by multiple projects. Often we want to include options/features in the template that most users wouldn't/shouldn't care about and just leave as default. Cases for this include:
* Features that are still not ready for general usage, and are still under development/debugging.
* Features that you'd want to leave the default 90% of the time (for e.g. the python version to compile the docs with, in almost all cases, it's the same as the project's version, but some projects need this to be different)

Currently, standard users have to consider these questions when copying/updating into a project, leaving them frustrated since they need to fill out a lot of redundant paperwork, but still stay vigilant since they don't know which questions are important or not ahead of time.

### Desired Situation

Ideally, users would like to automatically skip these "advanced" questions, leaving them at their default value until they explicitly need to use them.

### Proposed solution

I propose adding a new key to question in `copier.yml`: `ask`. `ask` acts the same as the existing `when` key, with the exception that questions marked as `ask: false` will still be prompted if the user's `copy` or `update` command has the `--ask` flag targeting the question. Specifically:

* If a question's `when` evaluates to `false`, the question will not be asked, regardless of the command's `--ask` filters, same as current behavior.
* Otherwise, If a question matches the command's `--ask` filters, it will prompt the user to answer, same as any other question.
* Otherwise, if a question's `ask` evaluates to `false`, it will be automatically skipped, and its default/previous value, if any, will be used to render the template (same as when its `when` key evaluates to `false`)

Example:
```yaml
# copier.yml
main_branch: 'main'
docs:
  type: bool
docs_branch:
  when: "{{ docs }}"  # question is only relevant if docs are enabled
  ask: false          # but most users still don't wanna fiddle with this
                      # even if docs are enabled
  default: "{{ main_branch }}"
release_branch:
  ask: "{{ main_branch != 'main' }}  # users only want to fiddle with
                                     # this if they're not using a standard
                                     # main branch. In this usage, "ask"
                                     # is like an opt-in "when"
```

```bash
>>> copier copy gh:my_template .
# will prompt main_branch, docs, and release_branch if main_branch != main
>>> copier copy gh:my_template . --ask release_branch
# will prompt main_branch, docs, and release_branch
>>> copier copy gh:my_template . --ask docs_branch
# will prompt main_branch, docs, and release_branch if main_branch != main,
#  if `docs` is true, will also prompt docs-branch
>>> copier copy gh:my_template . --ask '*_branch'
# will prompt main_branch, docs, and release_branch,
#  if `docs` is true, will also prompt docs-branch
```

problem_statement.title: views with star-select semantics and config 'view_update_via_alter' are not being updated
problem_statement.body:
The current v2 view materialization combined with an enabled `view_update_via_alter` config uses a changeset to determine when to actually run the `ALTER VIEW` command versus running a no-op (the other code paths will lead to unconditional `CREATE OR REPLACE` runs). The `QueryProcessor` component and its underlying `QueryConfig` will only detect changes when the actual SQL has changed. This poses an issue for views that use star select semantics, as schema changes in the queried tables will not be picked up by the diff and leading to stale views.

### Steps To Reproduce
1. materialize the following `seed.csv`:
```csv
id,msg
1,hello
```
2. run the following view model:
```sql
{{
    config(
        materialized='view',
        view_update_via_alter=True,
    )
}}
select * from {{ ref('seed') }};
```
3. update `seed.csv` and rerun:
```csv
id,msg,extra
1,hello,ben
```
4. rerun the view model: the column `extra` will not be added.

### Expected behavior
View materialization should update the schema, even if implicit via start select semantic.

problem_statement.title: Faster freeze of dense constraints into `CSRConstraint`
problem_statement.body:
> [!NOTE]
> The following content was generated by AI.

## Describe the feature you'd like to see

Child of #972 (phase 2, PR 6). This also helps dense models with `freeze=True`.

In a sparse model, most constraints still start as dense expressions. Variable bounds and storage balances are examples. `CSRConstraint.from_dense` (`linopy/constraints.py:1590-1660`) converts them, and this conversion is the largest remaining cost on the build side.

```python
import pandas as pd, linopy
linopy.options["semantics"] = "v1"
m = linopy.Model(sparse=True)
y = m.add_variables(0, 1, coords=[pd.RangeIndex(2000, name="i"), pd.RangeIndex(720, name="t")])
m.add_constraints(y <= 1)  # 1.44M one-term rows: about 90 ms
```

A direct conversion from the term rectangle to CSR (a mask plus `cumsum`, no sort) builds the same matrix in about 36 ms.

Where the time goes:

- `_matrix_export_data` (`linopy/constraints.py:2147-2173`) makes several reshape and fancy-index copies. Its peak memory is about 4 times the size of the result.
- `sum_duplicates` sorts each row, even when every row has only one term and is therefore already canonical.
- `np.unique` over the per-row sign array checks whether all signs are equal.

### Proposed direction

- Ravel `vars` and `coeffs` once, keep `vars != -1` and `coeffs != 0`, and build `indptr` with `cumsum`.
- Canonicalise (sort and sum duplicates) only when `nterm > 1`. `CSRConstraint` must still promise label-ordered rows (v1 canonical form).
- Check for a uniform sign with `(sign == sign[0]).all()`.
- Zero policy stays the same: zeros are dropped at freeze.
- Tests: frozen against dense equality for duplicate variables, explicit zeros, masked rows and mixed signs, using the existing helpers in `test/test_csr.py`.

<details>
<summary>Measurements</summary>

| case | time | peak memory |

problem_statement.title: TOML command references drop ignore/invert exit-code prefixes
problem_statement.body:
## Issue

Native TOML command references lose the `-` (ignore nonzero exit) and `!` (invert exit result) prefixes. Those prefixes are stored as `Command` flags, but a referenced command is reconstructed from its `.args` alone. As a result, a command that should be ignored can fail a referenced environment, and an inverted command can produce a false green result.

This is the TOML reference path, distinct from the INI prefix issue #3856 (fixed in #3748). The command-list conversion from #4112 also retains this behavior.

## Environment

- macOS arm64; Python 3.11.16.
- Current `main` at `f2749b7a5a74ac26a70c617c83f02efea8aaa640` (local development build 4.66.1.dev1).

## Minimal example

```toml
[env_run_base]
package = "skip"

[env.original]
commands = [["-", "python", "-c", "raise SystemExit(1)"]]

[env.referenced]
commands = { replace = "ref", env = "original", key = "commands" }
```

Run `tox run --no-provision -e original,referenced`.

Expected: both environments succeed because the referenced command retains its ignore-exit prefix. Actual on current main: `original: OK`, `referenced: FAIL code 1`, overall exit 1. The analogous `!` reference also loses inversion.

I have a narrow local patch and 18 regression cases: 12 new cases fail on the unchanged base, all 18 pass with the patch, and 281 adjacent tests pass. Would a PR for this TOML-specific correction be welcome? AI assistance was used in reproduction, patching, and independent review.

problem_statement.title: Memory leak: DedupeIntegration pins exception tracebacks in asyncio apps
problem_statement.body: ### How do you use Sentry? Self-hosted/on-premise ### Version 2.56.0 (Python 3.12.6) ### Steps to Reproduce 1. `sentry_sdk.init` with only `LoggingIntegration` + `DedupeIntegration` enabled. 2. In a long-lived asyncio task: build a local variable of ~1 MB so the frame carries that much data, raise `ValueError`, log with `logger.exception(...)`, keep the task running. 3. The exception, its traceback, and the 1 MB local stay alive for the lifetime of the task (and maybe after its death) ### Expected Result After `logger.exception(...)` returns and the `except` block exits, the exception, its traceback, and all its frame locals become unreachable and memory are freed ### Actual Result The exception stays alive for the whole lifetime of the task. Memory grows with every new captured exception on a new task, and the 1 MB local (plus the whole traceback chain) stays pinned until the task itself ends. RAM usage growth: ## What I found `DedupeIntegration._last_seen` is a `ContextVar` that stores the last captured exception. The SDK tries to store it as `weakref.ref(exc)`, but Python builtins (`ValueError`, `TypeError`, `KeyError`, ...) do not support weakref. On `TypeError` the SDK falls back to a strong reference Under asyncio every long-lived task keeps its own `ContextVar` state, so the strong reference lives as long as the task. Through that reference the SDK pins: - the exception, - `exc.__traceback__`, - every frame local in the traceback. In our web crawler frame locals held response payloads in the 500 KB-1 MB range, which is where the RSS growth came from ## Fix (what I did) Replace the dedupe processor with one that stores `weakref.ref(exc)` when possible and silently skips on `TypeError`. Dedupe is lost for builtins, leak is gone

problem_statement.title: `sqlfluff fix` deletes source text when a token spans a Jinja tag
problem_statement.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

`sqlfluff fix` deletes source text when a token spans a Jinja tag. A token spans a tag when the rendered SQL joins the text on both sides of the tag. For example, `b{% if true %}c{% endif %}` renders as the one identifier `bc`.

A fix deletes the part of such a token before the tag in two cases:

- The fix puts a new segment directly before the token. LT02 does this in q1.sql, and LT05 does it in q3.sql and q4.sql.
- The fix changes another segment in the same clause. In q2.sql, LT01 removes the spaces before the comma. The space before `b` does not change, but the `b` is deleted. `select b{% if true %}c{% endif %}, a  , x` loses its `b` too, with the fix after the token.

`sqlfluff fix` reports the violation as fixed and exits with 0. After the fix, `sqlfluff lint` with the same rule reports nothing.

I found this with LT05 and a skipped `{% if false %}` block. A skipped block is not necessary. LT01 and LT02 delete text in the same way with `{% if true %}`.

### Expected Behaviour

`sqlfluff fix` keeps all source text which is not whitespace. For q1.sql below, the expected output is:

```sql
select
    b{% if true %}c{% endif %}
```

For q2.sql it is `select a, b{% if true %}c{% endif %}`. If a fix cannot keep the text, `sqlfluff fix` does not apply it and reports the violation as unfixable.

### Observed Behaviour

Each command in "How to reproduce" prints `FIXED` for its files and exits with 0. The files are then:

q1.sql loses the `b`:

```sql
select
    {% if true %}c{% endif %}
```

q2.sql loses the `b`:

```sql
select a, {% if true %}c{% endif %}
```

q3.sql loses the comment `-- trailing comment here`:

```sql
select a, b, c
from tbl
{% if false %} xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx{% endif %}
```

q4.sql loses the 65 `a` characters:

```sql
{% if false %}
    select
{% endif %}select 1
```

`sqlfluff render` shows the column `bc` in q1.sql and q2.sql before the fix, and `c` after it. With the default rules, q1.sql, q3.sql and q4.sql lose the same text. q2.sql instead gets a second `{% if true %}` tag, and `sqlfluff render` then fails with `Failed to parse Jinja syntax`.

q3.sql is the `trailing_comment` test input in #8605. `main` without #8605 gives the same output, so the loss does not come from #8605.

**Cause.** The lexer yields the placeholder for a tag before the token which spans the tag. The code is `_iter_segments` in `src/sqlfluff/core/parser/lexer.py`. The placeholder and its indent or dedent meta then sit between the whitespace and the token. Their templated position is after the start of the token. Two functions use that position as the end of a source range, so the range covers the start of the token:

- `BaseSegment._position_segments` in `src/sqlfluff/core/parser/segments/base.py` positions a new segment up to the next sibling with a position. In q1.sql, the new indent from LT02 gets source slice `7:8`, which is the `b`. The new newline from LT05 gets source slice `23:49` in q3.sql and `20:86` in q4.sql.
- `_iter_templated_patches` in `src/sqlfluff/core/linter/patch.py` walks into each parent segment which has a change. It treats the gap before the placeholder as a deletion. In q2.sql, the parent is the `select_clause`. It yields a `mid_point` patch for source slice `12:13`, which is the `b`.

#7582 added a guard at both places for #6261. The guard skips only a `templated` placeholder which renders to an empty string. Here the placeholder is for a `block_start` or `block_end` tag. `generate_source_patches` then keeps the patch, because its source slice is inside one literal slice. In q3.sql and q4.sql, the token spans the tag only in the variant which renders the `{% if false %}` block.

The guard does not cover a Jinja comment either. With LT01, `select a  , b{# note #}c` loses its `b`. A `{% set x = 1 %}` tag gives a `templated` placeholder, and the guard keeps the `b`. The indent or dedent meta of the tag has the same templated position as its placeholder. With the guard widened to `block_start`, `block_end` and `comment` placeholders, q2.sql and q4.sql still lose their text.

### How to reproduce

```sh
cat > q1.sql <<'EOF'
select
b{% if true %}c{% endif %}
EOF
cat > q2.sql <<'EOF'
select a  , b{% if true %}c{% endif %}
EOF
cat > q3.sql <<'EOF'
select a, b, c from tbl  -- trailing comment here{% if false %} xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx{% endif %}
EOF
cat > q4.sql <<'EOF'
{% if false %}select aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa{% endif %}select 1
EOF
sqlfluff fix --dialect ansi --rules LT02 q1.sql
sqlfluff fix --dialect ansi --rules LT01 q2.sql
sqlfluff fix --dialect ansi --rules LT05 q3.sql q4.sql
```

### Dialect

ansi. postgres, bigquery, snowflake and tsql give the same output for q1.sql and q2.sql.

### Version

```
sqlfluff, version 4.3.0
Python 3.12.14
```

Measured on `main` at `2e2275713`. The `4.3.0` tag gives the same output for the four files.

### Configuration

None. There is no `.sqlfluff` file. The command line gives the dialect and the rule, and the templater is the default `jinja`.

### Are you willing to work on and submit a PR to address the issue?

- [x] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

### Code of Conduct

- [x] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)

problem_statement.title: Event persister stops flushing forever after a database outage (CancelledError ends flush_periodically)
problem_statement.body:
### Bug summary

After a short PostgreSQL outage (DB host reboot) the server keeps answering the API and accepting events, but no events are written to the database until the server is restarted. Event-based automations (e.g. proactive triggers on `prefect.flow-run.heartbeat`) silently stop firing.

Cause, in `src/prefect/server/events/services/event_persister.py` (identical in 3.8.0, 3.8.6, 3.8.7 and `main` as of 2026-10-06):

```python
async def flush_periodically():
    try:
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(flush_every.total_seconds())
            if queue.qsize():
                await flush()
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        return
```

`flush()` catches `Exception` around `db.session_context()` / `write_events` / `commit`, but during a database outage the DB driver can surface `asyncio.CancelledError` (a `BaseException`). It escapes `flush()`, is caught by `flush_periodically`, and the periodic task returns for good. Nothing restarts it; the only remaining flush path is the `batch_size` trigger in `message_handler`. The batch already taken out of the queue is lost too.

The same pattern was fixed for `TaskRunRecorder` in #22441 (issue #21057), but not for the event persister.

Steps to reproduce:
1. Run `prefect server start` against PostgreSQL (3.8.x).
2. Make PostgreSQL unavailable for about a minute (we hit it by rebooting the DB host), then bring it back.
3. POST a probe event to `/api/events`, then look it up by id via `/api/events/filter` — it is never found. Flow-run heartbeats are no longer stored; proactive automations do not fire.
4. Restart the server — events are written again.

### Version info

```Text
Version:              3.8.0
API version:          0.8.4
Python version:       3.14.6
Git commit:           218fb466
Built:                Thu, Jul 23, 2026 09:51 PM
OS/Arch:              linux/aarch64
Server type:          server
Pydantic version:     2.13.4
Server:
  Database:           postgresql (17)

Also seen on 3.8.6 in a second installation; the code is unchanged in 3.8.7 and main.
```

### Additional context

Expected: the periodic flush survives database errors (retry / back off) and only exits when the service itself is being stopped — e.g. tell our own cancellation apart from a CancelledError raised inside flush(), or restart the task when it ends unexpectedly.

Workaround we run: a timer every 5 minutes posts a probe event and looks it up by id; if it is not stored within a minute, the server is restarted.

problem_statement.title: `os.path.basename`, `os.path.splitext` and `os.path.commonpath` don't work under Windows simulation
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**
With Windows simulated on a POSIX host, `os.path.basename`, `os.path.splitext` and `os.path.commonpath` don't behave like they do on Windows. They only split on `/`, so backslash-separated paths come back wrong. `os.path.split`, `join`, `dirname` and `normpath` give the right answers for the same paths.

Expected: the same results as on Windows.

```
os.path.split('C:\\a/foo\\t.x')               -> ('C:\\a/foo', 't.x')    (correct)
os.path.basename('C:\\a/foo\\t.x')            -> 'foo\\t.x'              (expected 't.x')
os.path.basename('C:\\a\\foo\\t.x')           -> 'C:\\a\\foo\\t.x'       (expected 't.x')
os.path.splitext('C:\\a.b\\foo')              -> ('C:\\a', '.b\\foo')    (expected ('C:\\a.b\\foo', ''))
os.path.commonpath(['C:\\a\\b', 'C:/a\\c'])   -> ''                      (expected 'C:\\a')
```

**How To Reproduce**
Run on a POSIX host. This prints each result next to what `ntpath` returns for the same input:

```python
import ntpath
import os
from pyfakefs.fake_filesystem import OSType
from pyfakefs.fake_filesystem_unittest import Patcher

cases = [
    ('split', ('C:\\a/foo\\t.x',)),
    ('basename', ('C:\\a/foo\\t.x',)),
    ('basename', ('C:\\a\\foo\\t.x',)),
    ('splitext', ('C:\\a.b\\foo',)),
    ('commonpath', (['C:\\a\\b', 'C:/a\\c'],)),
]
# real ntpath results, computed before the Patcher is active
expected = [getattr(ntpath, name)(*args) for name, args in cases]

with Patcher() as p:
    p.fs.os = OSType.WINDOWS
    for (name, args), want in zip(cases, expected):
        got = getattr(os.path, name)(*args)
        print(f"os.path.{name}{args}: {got!r}  ntpath: {want!r}  {'' if got == want else 'DIFFERS'}")
```

Output:
```
os.path.split('C:\\a/foo\\t.x',): ('C:\\a/foo', 't.x')  ntpath: ('C:\\a/foo', 't.x')  
os.path.basename('C:\\a/foo\\t.x',): 'foo\\t.x'  ntpath: 't.x'  DIFFERS
os.path.basename('C:\\a\\foo\\t.x',): 'C:\\a\\foo\\t.x'  ntpath: 't.x'  DIFFERS
os.path.splitext('C:\\a.b\\foo',): ('C:\\a', '.b\\foo')  ntpath: ('C:\\a.b\\foo', '')  DIFFERS
os.path.commonpath(['C:\\a\\b', 'C:/a\\c'],): ''  ntpath: 'C:\\a'  DIFFERS
```

**Your environment**
```
macOS-27.0-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O
Python 3.14.7 (main, Aug  5 2026, 10:29:49) [Clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)]
pyfakefs 6.2.0
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pytest'
```

problem_statement.title: [Bug]: REST client raises AttributeError when an HTTP error body is not a google.rpc.Status
problem_statement.body:
### What happened?

When a REST call fails with an HTTP error whose JSON body is not a `google.rpc.Status` object, `RestTransport` raises a bare `AttributeError` instead of an A2A client error. This is common when the response comes from a proxy or gateway rather than the agent, e.g. an OAuth layer answering `401` with `{"error": "invalid_token"}` (RFC 6750), or a load balancer answering `502` with a JSON string.

`_parse_rest_error` (`src/a2a/client/transports/rest.py`) assumes `payload["error"]` is an object:

```python
error_data = error_payload.get('error', {})
message = error_data.get('message', fallback_message)  # str / list / None -> AttributeError
```

`_handle_http_error` only catches `JSONDecodeError`/`ValueError`, so the status-based fallback below it (`MethodNotFoundError` for 404, `A2AClientError` otherwise) never runs. Streaming calls fail the same way. The v0.3 compat REST transport has the same problem in its `_handle_http_error` (`error_data.get('type')` on a non-object body).

### Reproduction (main @ dac7d9d)

```python
import asyncio, httpx
from a2a.client.transports.rest import RestTransport
from a2a.types.a2a_pb2 import AgentCard, GetTaskRequest

async def main():
    client = httpx.AsyncClient(transport=httpx.MockTransport(
        lambda r: httpx.Response(401, json={"error": "invalid_token"})))
    await RestTransport(client, AgentCard(), "http://agent").get_task(GetTaskRequest(id="t1"))

asyncio.run(main())
# AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'
```

| Status | Body | Raised | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 401 | `{"error": "invalid_token"}` | `AttributeError` | `A2AClientError` |
| 404 | `{"error": "Not Found"}` | `AttributeError` | `MethodNotFoundError` |
| 502 | `["bad gateway"]` | `AttributeError` | `A2AClientError` |
| 500 | `"Internal Server Error"` | `AttributeError` | `A2AClientError` |
| 503 | `null` | `AttributeError` | `A2AClientError` |

A well-formed `google.rpc.Status` body still maps correctly (e.g. `TASK_NOT_FOUND` → `TaskNotFoundError`).

### Expected

Bodies that are not a `google.rpc.Status` are ignored, and the existing HTTP-status fallback applies. I have a small fix with regression tests ready and will open a PR.

problem_statement.title: [Bug]: DefaultRequestHandler runs follow-up messages on a task with the first request's contextvars
problem_statement.body:
### What happened?

With `DefaultRequestHandler` (v2), a follow-up message on an existing task runs `AgentExecutor.execute()` with the contextvars of the request that **created** the task, not the request that sent the follow-up. A common case is a reply after the task went `input-required`.

Any per-request contextvar set by ASGI middleware or by the `ServerCallContextBuilder` comes through stale: auth tokens, tenant or caller identity, request-scoped tracing. `ServerCallContext.state` is correct per message. Only contextvars are wrong.

Reproduced on 1.1.2 and 1.2.2, for both `SendMessage` and `SendStreamingMessage`. 0.3.x is not affected because its handler started a new producer per message.

### Cause

`ActiveTask.start()` creates the producer with `asyncio.create_task(self._run_producer())` during the first request, so the producer copies that request's context once. Later requests call `ActiveTask.enqueue_request()`, which only puts the `RequestContext` on `_request_queue`. The producer then calls `execute()` from the first request's context. A task parked in `input-required` keeps its `ActiveTask` (#1296), so a reply hours later still sees the first request's values, which may by then be an expired token.

### Reproduction

```python
import asyncio, contextvars, uuid

import httpx
from a2a.helpers import new_task_from_user_message
from a2a.server.agent_execution import AgentExecutor
from a2a.server.request_handlers import DefaultRequestHandler
from a2a.server.routes import create_jsonrpc_routes
from a2a.server.tasks import InMemoryTaskStore, TaskUpdater
from a2a.types import AgentCapabilities, AgentCard
from starlette.applications import Starlette

REQUEST_TAG = contextvars.ContextVar("request_tag", default="unset")


class TagMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, app):
        self.app = app

    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
        token = REQUEST_TAG.set(dict(scope.get("headers", [])).get(b"x-tag", b"unset").decode())
        try:
            await self.app(scope, receive, send)
        finally:
            REQUEST_TAG.reset(token)


class Executor(AgentExecutor):
    async def execute(self, context, event_queue):
        print(f"execute({context.get_user_input()!r}) sees request_tag={REQUEST_TAG.get()!r}")
        task = context.current_task or new_task_from_user_message(context.message)
        updater = TaskUpdater(event_queue, task.id, task.context_id)
        if context.current_task:
            await updater.complete()
        else:

app.add_middleware(TagMiddleware)


async def send(client, tag, text, task=None):
    message = {"messageId": str(uuid.uuid4()), "role": "ROLE_USER", "parts": [{"text": text}]}
    if task:
        message |= {"taskId": task["id"], "contextId": task["contextId"]}
    body = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "SendMessage", "params": {"message": message}}
    resp = await client.post("/", json=body, headers={"x-tag": tag, "A2A-Version": "1.0"})

async def main():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=httpx.ASGITransport(app=app), base_url="http://t") as client:

```

Actual:

```
execute('book a flight') sees request_tag='request-1'
execute('Friday') sees request_tag='request-1'
```

Expected:

```
execute('book a flight') sees request_tag='request-1'
execute('Friday') sees request_tag='request-2'
```

### Proposed fix

Capture the sender's context in `enqueue_request()` and run `execute()` in it:

```python
async def enqueue_request(self, request_context):
    request_id = uuid.uuid4()
    await self._request_queue.put((request_context, request_id, contextvars.copy_context()))
    return request_id

# in _run_producer()
request_context, request_id, sender_context = await self._request_queue.get()
...
await sender_context.run(
    asyncio.create_task,
    self._agent_executor.execute(request_context, self._event_queue_agent),
)
```

I applied this patch to 1.2.2 locally and the reproduction prints `request-2` for the follow-up, for both `SendMessage` and `SendStreamingMessage`. `Context.run(asyncio.create_task, ...)` works on Python 3.10. Awaiting the child task keeps cancellation working, because cancelling the producer cancels the child. The MCP Python SDK fixed the same problem this way in modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk#2298.

### Downstream workaround

bedrock-agentcore works around this today without touching a2a internals. It wraps `SimpleRequestContextBuilder` to store `contextvars.copy_context()` in `call_context.state`, and wraps the executor to run `execute()` in that copy (aws/bedrock-agentcore-sdk-python#690). A fix here would let downstream projects delete that code, and it would also cover users who build `DefaultRequestHandler` directly.

problem_statement.title: AudioInterface.set_aligned_starting_time raises on a second call for a single audio file; add_acoustic_waveform_series returns None
problem_statement.body:
Two small problems in the audio path.

`AudioInterface.set_aligned_starting_time` handles two cases: no starting times yet with one file, where it sets them, and starting times already present with several files, where it shifts them. Everything else raises. That leaves out the single-file interface whose starting time is already set, so a second call, or a call after `set_aligned_segment_starting_times`, raises instead of shifting:

```python
interface = AudioInterface(file_paths=[one_file])
interface.set_aligned_starting_time(1.0)
interface.set_aligned_starting_time(0.5)
# ValueError: There are no segment starting times to shift by a common value!
```

The other interfaces treat `set_aligned_starting_time` as a shift that accumulates, and the error message here describes a situation that is not the one it fires in. The branch condition should shift whenever starting times exist, whatever the file count.

`add_acoustic_waveform_series` is annotated `-> NWBFile` and its docstring says it returns the file passed in, but only the early "already in nwbfile" branch returns it; the normal path falls off the end and returns `None`. The interface ignores the return value, so nothing in the repo is affected, but a caller following the signature gets `None`.

+    assert _dump_context(agent.state.context) == original_dump
+    assert agent.formatter._qwenpaw_force_strip_media is False
+

+@pytest.mark.asyncio

+    ("wire_media_count", "has_formatter"),
+    [(0, True), (1, False)],
+    ids=["no-wire-media", "no-formatter"],

+    agent.formatter = _formatter(wire_media_count)

+    async def provider_reasoning(self, tool_choice=None):
+        nonlocal calls

+            pass
+
+    assert calls == 1

problem_statement.title: Oversized image stored in context makes a session permanently unusable
problem_statement.body:
## What happened

A conversation died permanently after an image passed through it.

I was generating a report and having it send an image out. The image was
taller than what the provider accepts, so the provider rejected that request.
Every later message in the same conversation then failed with the same 400 —
including plain-text turns that carried no media at all. The offending image
block is stored in the session context and replayed on every subsequent
request, so the conversation never recovered on its own and stayed unusable.

The only way out was to repair the stored session file by hand.

## Expected

A media payload the provider refuses should cost the media, not the
conversation: the request retries without it, and the stored context is
repaired so later turns go through.

## Why it cannot self-heal today

The rejection matches none of the recovery branches in
`react_agent._reasoning`:

- it does not name the model's capability, so
  `_is_explicit_media_capability_error()` returns `False`;
- in some wordings it also names no size/pixel/limit signal, so the
  request-scoped handling never engages either.

`_reasoning` therefore re-raises, and because the block is still sitting in
the stored context it is replayed forever — the same 400 on every turn,
permanently.

DeepSeek is a concrete case. An image whose side exceeds 8192 px is answered
with:

```
You have uploaded an unsupported image. Please make sure your image is valid
and has one of the following formats: webp, png, jpeg, and gif.
```

That message names neither the limit nor the model's capability, so nothing
classifies it as recoverable.

## Note

`_REQUEST_SCOPED_MEDIA_LIMIT_SIGNALS` already documents that these errors
"may justify a media-free retry, but must never poison the model-wide
`rejects_media` cache" — but no code implements that retry. A PR adding the
missing branch follows.

+def _vlen_string_chunk_shape(dataset: H5Dataset) -> tuple[int, ...]:
+    """
+    Chunk shape for a variable-length string dataset, whose chunks are inlined.
+
+    The HDF5 chunk shape is kept, but trimmed to the array shape: an inlined
+    chunk is re-encoded, so unlike a referenced chunk (see ``_chunk_shape``)
+    trimming it is always safe.
+    """
+    shape = dataset.shape
+    chunks = dataset.chunks if dataset.chunks is not None else shape
+    return tuple(max(min(c, s), 1) for c, s in zip(chunks, shape))
+
+
+def _inlined_vlen_string_manifest(
+    dataset: H5Dataset,
+    *,
+    chunks: tuple[int, ...],
+    fill_value: str | None,
+) -> ChunkManifest:
+    """
+    Read an HDF5 variable-length string dataset into inlined chunks.
+
+    Each chunk is read with h5py and encoded the way the zarr ``vlen-utf8`` codec
+    encodes it. An edge chunk is padded to the full chunk shape with the fill
+    value, as zarr does when writing. A dataset with no allocated storage gets an
+    empty manifest, so it reads as the fill value.
+
+    Parameters
+    ----------
+    dataset
+        An h5py variable-length string dataset, of either character set.
+    chunks
+        The chunk shape, as returned by ``_vlen_string_chunk_shape``.
+    fill_value
+        The array's fill value.
+
+    Returns

+    ChunkManifest
+        A manifest in which every chunk is inlined.
+    """

+
+    shape = dataset.shape
+    if dataset.size == 0 or dataset.id.get_storage_size() == 0:
+        return ChunkManifest(entries={}, shape=shape)
+
+    codec = VLenUTF8()
+    strings = dataset.asstr()
+    pad = "" if fill_value is None else fill_value
+    grid_shape = tuple(math.ceil(s / c) for s, c in zip(shape, chunks))
+    inlined: dict[tuple[int, ...], bytes] = {}
+    for index in np.ndindex(grid_shape):
+        region = tuple(
+            slice(i * c, min((i + 1) * c, s)) for i, c, s in zip(index, chunks, shape)
+        )
+        values = np.asarray(strings[region], dtype=object)
+        chunk = np.full(chunks, pad, dtype=object)
+        # the trailing Ellipsis makes a 0-d assignment copy the element rather
+        # than store the 0-d array itself as an object
+        chunk[tuple(slice(0, n) for n in values.shape) + (...,)] = values
+        inlined[index] = codec.encode(np.ascontiguousarray(chunk))
+
+    lengths = np.zeros(grid_shape, dtype=np.uint64)
+    for index, data in inlined.items():
+        lengths[index] = len(data)
+    return ChunkManifest.from_arrays(
+        paths=np.full(grid_shape, INLINED_CHUNK_PATH, dtype=np.dtypes.StringDType()),  # type: ignore

+        lengths=lengths,

problem_statement.title: HDFParser: read variable-length string datasets at parse time as inlined chunks
problem_statement.body:
Split out of #1104, as @TomNicholas suggested there.

### Problem

`HDFParser` can't read HDF5 variable-length string datasets. Their chunks hold pointers into the HDF5 global heap, not the strings, so a virtual reference to them can't be decoded. Today the parser warns and virtualizes the metadata anyway. Reading the variable then fails, and so does `loadable_variables`, which reads the same chunks:

```python
with h5py.File("/tmp/strings.h5", "w") as f:
    f["labels"] = np.array(["a", "bb", "ccc"], dtype=h5py.string_dtype())

parse("/tmp/strings.h5", loadable_variables=["labels"])
# UserWarning: Variable '/labels' is an HDF5 variable-length string dataset. ...
# ValueError: corrupt buffer, data seem truncated
```

The only workaround is to find these datasets with h5py first, pass them to `drop_variables`, and read and write them separately. In some formats they're everywhere: every NWB file has several, for example.

### Proposal

Read the strings at parse time and store them as inlined chunks:

- Read each HDF5 chunk with h5py, using the HDF5 chunk shape trimmed to the array shape. Encode it the way Zarr's `vlen-utf8` codec does, padding an edge chunk with the fill value.
- Use `vlen-utf8` as the only codec. The HDF5 filters compress the heap pointers, not the strings.
- Keep an empty manifest for a dataset with no allocated storage, so it reads as the fill value.

`ChunkManifest` already supports inlined chunks, and the Icechunk and kerchunk writers already write them.

One related fix is needed for the kerchunk writer. `convert_v3_to_v2_metadata` drops every array-to-bytes codec, including `vlen-utf8`. A Zarr v2 string array needs `vlen-utf8` as its first filter, so a string array written to kerchunk currently can't be read.

I have a PR for this ready.

+            atexit.register(_release_mcp_writer_lock)

+        # collection. Drop it while ownership is held so the pending mutating

problem_statement.title: MCP kg_add leaks the palace mine lock on Windows (handle never released, blocks all mining)
problem_statement.body:
**What happened?**

On Windows, a `kg_add` call through the MCP server (`mempalace-mcp`) acquires the palace mine lock but never releases it after the write completes. The lock file `~/.mempalace/locks/mine_palace_<hash>.lock` is created at the exact timestamp of the `kg_add` call, and an open file handle is retained indefinitely by the MCP server process. Every subsequent `mempalace mine` then fails with "is held by" lock contention — permanently, until the MCP process is killed and the lock file deleted manually.

**What did you expect?**

The mine-palace lock should be released when the KG write finishes (the `kg_add` call returned success with a `triple_id`), leaving subsequent mines free to proceed.

**How to reproduce:**

1. Run opencode (or any MCP client) with `mempalace-mcp` configured, palace at default location.
2. Have the model call `mempalace_mempalace_kg_add` (I did 4 adds in quick succession).
3. Calls return success; note `~/.mempalace/locks/mine_palace_<hash>.lock` now exists, created at the same second/millisecond as the kg_add calls, content empty.
4. Trigger any `mempalace mine` (or let an automation hook run it) — it reports the palace lock "is held by" the (still-running) MCP process and keeps failing.
5. `Remove-Item <lock>` on Windows → "being used by another process" (handle genuinely held).
6. Kill the `mempalace-mcp` process tree → handle released → lock file deletable → mining works again.

**Evidence (from my incident):**

- Lock file `mine_palace_eeea0af05abc81a9.lock` LastWriteTime `02:14:29` local, matching MCP tool-call log entries at `18:14:29.103/.129/.152/.173Z` to the millisecond (4 × `kg_add`).
- Lock file content: empty.
- Windows deletion error: `The process cannot access the file ... because it is being used by another process`.
- After killing all `mempalace-mcp` processes: lock deletable, `mempalace mine` immediately succeeded.
- Possibly related: several `mempalace-mcp` python processes had wedged (accumulated ~16s CPU then zero activity for 10+ minutes) — the handle appears to be held by a process that is otherwise unresponsive.

**Environment:**

- OS: Windows 11 (10.0.26231), PowerShell 7
- Python version: 3.10 (uv-managed cpython `cpython-3.10-windows-x86_64-none`)
- MemPal version: 3.10.0 (`mempalace status` reports backend chroma / chromadb 1.5.9), installed via `uv tool install mempalace`
- MCP server: `mempalace-mcp` spawned by OpenCode V2 (opencode 2.0.19) via stdio

Thank you for the project — the rest of the pipeline (mining, search, KG queries) has been rock solid.

problem_statement.title: [BUG] r2_score is outside the zero_division design from #3132: a constant actual series scores NaN for a perfect forecast
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**

`r2_score` divides by its denominator without a guard (`darts/metrics/metrics.py:2508-2511`):

```python
ss_errors = np.nansum((y_true - y_pred) ** 2, axis=TIME_AX)
y_hat = np.nanmean(y_true, axis=TIME_AX)
ss_tot = np.nansum((y_true - y_hat) ** 2, axis=TIME_AX)
return 1 - ss_errors / ss_tot
```

`ss_tot` is zero whenever the actual series is constant, which is a normal thing to score: a flat segment, a sensor that did not move, a zero-inflated series.

#3132 records the agreed design for exactly this situation:

> * **0/0** (numerator 0 *and* denominator 0) → the metric's **best score** (a perfect forecast on a degenerate series)
> * **x/0** (numerator != 0, denominator 0) → `np.nan`. Filling with the best score here would mask a real miss.
> * `zero_division="raise"` preserves the legacy `ValueError`.

`r2_score` matches neither branch:

| case | agreed design | `r2_score` today | `sklearn.metrics.r2_score` |
|---|---|---|---|
| constant actual, exact forecast (0/0) | best score, i.e. `1.0` | `nan` | `1.0` |
| constant actual, wrong forecast (x/0) | `nan` | `-inf` | `0.0` |

It also does not accept `zero_division`, while `mape`, `ape`, `arre`, `marre`, `ope`, `wmape` and `coefficient_of_variation` all do.

Neither #3132 nor #3080 mentions R^2; the work was scoped to the percentage and range metrics, and `r2_score` appears to have been missed rather than deliberately excluded.

**To Reproduce**

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from darts import TimeSeries, metrics

ts = lambda v: TimeSeries.from_series(pd.Series(np.array(v, float), index=pd.RangeIndex(len(v))))

# a forecast that is exactly right, on a constant series
print(metrics.r2_score(ts([5., 5., 5., 5.]), ts([5., 5., 5., 5.])))   # nan
# a forecast that is wrong, on the same series
print(metrics.r2_score(ts([5., 5., 5., 5.]), ts([1., 2., 3., 4.])))   # -inf

metrics.r2_score(ts([5., 5., 5., 5.]), ts([5., 5., 5., 5.]), zero_division="raise")
# TypeError: r2_score() got an unexpected keyword argument 'zero_division'
```

**Expected behavior**

The design already agreed in #3132, applied to `r2_score`: route the division through the shared `_safe_divide` helper (`darts/metrics/utils.py:876`) and accept `zero_division` as the sibling metrics do. Note that the helper divides `ss_errors` by `ss_tot`, so the fill applies to the ratio rather than to R^2 itself: `zero_fill=0.0` is the value that makes the 0/0 case come out as R^2 = 1.0, the best score. `strict_zero=True` also looks right here, so that a genuinely small variance is not treated as zero. That gives `1.0` for the exact forecast, `nan` for the wrong one, and `ValueError` under `zero_division="raise"`, and it happens to agree with `sklearn` on the first two.

**Additional context**

Also reaches `backtest` and `gridsearch` when `metric=r2_score`, since one constant window makes the aggregate `nan` or `-inf`.

I have a fix and regression tests ready and would be happy to open the PR, if this reading of #3132 is the one you intended.

**System**

```
darts 0.47.0 (master @ 351b53e1) | python 3.13.3 | pandas 3.0.6 | numpy 2.5.3 | Linux x86_64
```

problem_statement.title: [BUG] row_to_names fails on slices without a start or a stop
problem_statement.body:
The docstring says `row_numbers` can be a slice, but slices without a start or a stop break:

```python
import polars as pl, pandas as pd, janitor, janitor.polars

pl.DataFrame({"a": ["x", "1"], "b": ["p", "2"]}).row_to_names(slice(None, 1))
# TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for -: 'int' and 'NoneType'

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": list("wxyz"), "b": list("1234")})
df.row_to_names(slice(None, 2), remove_rows_above=True)
# TypeError
df.row_to_names(slice(-2, None), remove_rows_above=True).shape
# (6, 2), from a 4 row frame
```

The polars version uses `row_numbers.start` and `row_numbers.stop` directly, and so do the `remove_rows_above` branches in pandas. Normalizing with `slice.indices()` fixes both. Happy to open a PR.

problem_statement.title: Normalize usage of `project_name`
problem_statement.body:
### What is the problem or limitation you are having?

Briefcase currently provides a global-level `project_name` configuration item.

This is currently a *required* item; however, it overlaps in purpose with the [required PEP 621 `name` key](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#declaring-project-metadata-the-project-table). 

### Describe the solution you'd like

If a project defines a top level PEP 621 `name` field, that should be used as the "project name", and be merged into the global configuration as part of the PEP 621 configuration merge step. The value that has been provided should be [validated and normalised](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/name-normalization/#names-and-normalization) as required by PEP 621.

If a project defines a `project_name` in the historical `[tool.briefcase]` format, that should continue to be accepted. However, if the provided value *cannot* be validated and normalised using PEP 621 rules, a warning should be raised (with a note that this may become an error in future).

In the new project wizard, the *app name* should be used as the default project name, not the formal name. The project name should be validated using the same rules as app name.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Fully deprecate and ignore the `project_name` field. It's not actually being used for anything, as Briefcase has no real "project" level concepts. However, PEP 621 is organised at the level of "projects", so we should retain that abstraction; for small projects, "project" and "app" can be the same thing.

### Additional context

This is part of the broader #1235 effort to move to PEP 621 configuration.

problem_statement.title: apply_voi() and apply_modality_lut() wrap out-of-range LUT indices instead of clamping them
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**

Both `apply_voi()` and `apply_modality_lut()` build the LUT index array with a dtype that is too narrow, and only clip *after* the values have been cast into it. Out-of-range input values therefore wrap around rather than being clamped, and `np.clip()` becomes a no-op. The result is silently wrong pixel values - no warning, no exception.

There are two separate ways this happens:

**1. `apply_voi()` - index dtype is taken from the LUT entry depth**

`clipped_iv` is allocated with the dtype derived from *LUT Descriptor* value 3 (bits per entry). For an 8-bit LUT that is `uint8`, so any input value above 255 wraps modulo 256. The number of entries is independent of the depth of each entry, so a 4096-entry LUT with 8-bit entries is perfectly legal - and it is the ordinary case for displaying 12-bit data on an 8-bit display.

```python
import numpy as np
from pydicom.dataset import Dataset
from pydicom.pixels import apply_voi

ds = Dataset()
item = Dataset()
item.LUTDescriptor = [4096, 0, 8]
item.LUTData = [idx // 16 for idx in range(4096)]
ds.VOILUTSequence = [item]

arr = np.asarray([0, 255, 256, 1024, 4095], dtype="uint16")
print(apply_voi(arr, ds))
```

Actual: `[ 0 15  0  0 15]`
Expected: `[  0  15  16  64 255]`

**2. `apply_modality_lut()` - index dtype is taken from the input array**

`clipped_iv` is allocated with `arr.dtype`, so `arr - first_map` can overflow before it is clipped. A negative *LUT Descriptor* value 2 is routine for CT, and shifts the values upward:

```python
import numpy as np
from pydicom.dataset import Dataset
from pydicom.pixels import apply_modality_lut

ds = Dataset()
item = Dataset()
item.LUTDescriptor = [4096, -2048, 16]
item.LUTData = list(range(4096))
ds.ModalityLUTSequence = [item]

arr = np.asarray([-2048, 0, 2047, 32767], dtype="int16")
print(apply_modality_lut(arr, ds))
```

Actual: `[   0 2048 4095    0]`
Expected: `[   0 2048 4095 4095]`

The last value overflows `int16` once 2048 is added, wraps negative, and is clamped to the *first* entry instead of the last.

**Expected behavior**

Input values above the last LUT index should map to the last entry, as PS3.3 C.11.1.1.1 and C.11.2.1.1 describe, regardless of the entry depth or the input dtype.

**Your environment**

module       | version
------       | -------
platform     | Windows-11-10.0.26200-SP0
Python       | 3.12.10
pydicom      | 3.1.0.dev0 (main, 60cebd0)
numpy        | 2.2.4

problem_statement.title: [http] seek() treats a failed range response as EOF instead of raising
problem_statement.body:
#### Problem description

`SeekableBufferedInputBase.seek()` silently swallows a non-OK range response (e.g. 503, 416, 403).
It closes the response, sets the position to the target anyway, and every following `read()` returns `b""`.
The caller sees a clean EOF, so the file looks shorter than it is and the data loss goes unnoticed.

The constructor raises on the same status via `raise_for_status()` (https://github.com/piskvorky/smart_open/blob/9bc1d45/smart_open/http.py#L181), so seek should too.
Expected: `seek()` raises `requests.HTTPError` and keeps the previous position, matching how a failed range request is handled since https://github.com/piskvorky/smart_open/pull/975.

Code: https://github.com/piskvorky/smart_open/blob/9bc1d45/smart_open/http.py#L361-L366

```python
if new_pos != self.content_length:
    response = self._partial_request(new_pos)
    if response.ok:
        self.response = response
    else:
        response.close()

self._current_pos = new_pos
```

Suggested fix: close the response, then `response.raise_for_status()` before touching `self._current_pos`.

#### Steps/code to reproduce the problem

```python
import responses
import smart_open

URL = "http://example.com/file"

with responses.RequestsMock(assert_all_requests_are_fired=False) as rsps:
    rsps.add(responses.GET, URL, body=bytes(range(32)), headers={"Accept-Ranges": "bytes"})
    rsps.add(responses.GET, URL, status=503)
    with smart_open.open(URL, "rb", transport_params={"buffer_size": 4}) as f:
        print(f.read(1))  # b'\x00'
        print(f.seek(16))  # 16, no error
        print(f.read())  # b'', expected HTTPError on seek
```

#### Versions

develop at 9bc1d45 (after https://github.com/piskvorky/smart_open/pull/975), Python 3.10, macOS.

#### Checklist

- [x] Described the problem clearly
- [x] Provided a minimal reproducible example, including any required data
- [x] Provided the version numbers of the relevant software

             text = token.evolve(value="{}", implicit_value=UNSET)
@@ -1020,6 +1021,42 @@ def _takes_mapping(hint: Any) -> bool:
     return hint is Any or is_structured_type(hint) or is_class_and_subclass(get_origin(hint) or hint, Mapping)
 
 
+def _call_value_converter(cparam: Any, type_: Any, tokens: Any) -> Any:
+    """Invoke a type's own ``Parameter`` converter over the value's tokens.
+
+    Mirrors how :class:`.Argument` invokes a parameter-level converter:
+    bound methods receive only the tokens; other callables receive ``(type, tokens)``.
+    """
+    resolved_converter = cparam.resolve_converter(type_)
+    assert resolved_converter is not None  # Caller checked that a converter is set.
+    if inspect.ismethod(resolved_converter):
+        return resolved_converter(tokens)
+    return resolved_converter(type_, tokens)
+
+
+def _apply_validators(type_: Any, value: Any) -> Any:
+    """Run the ``Parameter`` validators annotated on ``type_`` against an already-converted ``value``.
+
+    Some conversion paths in :func:`_convert_entry` (dictionary values, empty containers)
+    do not pass through :func:`_convert`, so they must apply a type's own validators
+    themselves; this mirrors the validator handling at the end of :func:`_convert`.
+    """
+    from cyclopts.parameter import Parameter
+
+    bare_type, cparam = Parameter.from_annotation(type_)
+    try:
+        for validator in cparam.validator:  # pyright: ignore
+            if isinstance(validator, str):
+                validator = getattr(bare_type, validator)
+            if inspect.ismethod(validator):

problem_statement.title: Parameter metadata on a container value type in dict[str, ...] is ignored
problem_statement.body:
A dict whose value type is a container with its own `Parameter` metadata silently ignores that metadata. Here the validator runs for the top-level parameter but never for the dict value:

```python
from typing import Annotated

import cyclopts
from cyclopts import App, Parameter
from cyclopts.config import Dict


def reject_empty(type_, value):
    print(f"validator called with {value!r}")
    if not value:
        raise ValueError("must not be empty")


Ids = Annotated[list[int], Parameter(validator=reject_empty)]

top = App(config=Dict({"x": [1]}), result_action="return_value")


@top.default
def main_top(x: Ids):
    return x


nested = App(config=Dict({"x": {"k": [1]}}), result_action="return_value")


@nested.default
def main_nested(x: dict[str, Ids]):
    return x


print(cyclopts.__version__)
print("top:", top([]))
print("nested:", nested([]))
```

```
5.2.0
validator called with [1]
top: [1]
nested: {'k': [1]}
```

A value-type `Parameter(converter=...)` is ignored the same way. Scalar value types work (e.g. `dict[str, PositiveInt]`), because only the scalar dispatch at the end of `_convert_entry` re-attaches the stashed `annotations_`; the iterable (`convert_priv(type_, tokens)`) and nested-dict branches pass the resolved type with the metadata stripped. Probably the same `convert()` vs `_convert()` metadata-survival issue as before, just for container-valued entries.

Found while reviewing #993 (Copilot flagged it for the empty-value early return, but the non-empty path has the same gap).

+def _make_image_series_paths_relative_to_nwbfile(nwbfile: NWBFile, nwbfile_path: Path) -> None:
+    """
+    Rewrite every ``ImageSeries.external_file`` entry so it is relative to the directory of ``nwbfile_path``.
+
+    The NWB specification reads ``external_file`` relative to the NWB file, while interfaces store whatever
+    path the caller handed them, which is usually absolute or relative to the working directory. An
+    ``ImageSeries`` read from an existing file is left alone, since its entries are already relative to that
+    file and not to the working directory. URLs are left as they are, and an entry that has no relative path
+    to the output at all (on Windows, a file on another drive) is written absolute. The result always uses
+    forward slashes so it stays meaningful once the file leaves the machine that wrote it.
+    """
+    output_directory = Path(nwbfile_path).resolve().parent
+    # `nwbfile.objects` is built on its first read and never invalidated, so it does not hold anything added
+    # to the file afterwards. `all_children` recomputes the walk.
+    for neurodata_object in nwbfile.all_children():
+        if not isinstance(neurodata_object, ImageSeries) or not neurodata_object.external_file:
+            continue
+        if neurodata_object.container_source is not None:  # read from disk, so already relative to that file
+            continue
+        rewritten_entries = []
+        for entry in neurodata_object.external_file:
+            entry = str(entry)  # an interface may have stored a `Path`
+            absolute_entry = Path(entry).resolve()
+            is_url = "://" in entry
+            if is_url:
+                rewritten_entries.append(entry)
+                continue
+            is_on_another_drive = absolute_entry.anchor != output_directory.anchor  # Windows: no relative path exists
+            if is_on_another_drive:
+                rewritten_entries.append(absolute_entry.as_posix())
+                continue
+            # TODO: replace with `absolute_entry.relative_to(output_directory, walk_up=True)` once the Python
+            # floor is 3.12; before that `Path.relative_to` cannot produce `..` segments.
+            rewritten_entries.append(Path(os.path.relpath(absolute_entry, start=output_directory)).as_posix())
+        # The setter refuses a field that is already set, and the list itself may belong to the interface that
+        # built the series, so a new list goes in where the setter would have stored it.
+        neurodata_object.fields["external_file"] = rewritten_entries
+

problem_statement.title: [feature] Pass original URL as a header when downloading sources from backup URLs
problem_statement.body:
### What is your suggestion?

When conan downloads sources from the backup URL, I would like the original URL to be passed as a header. Maybe something like `X-Resource-Original-Url: https://example.com/libfoo.tar.gz`.

This can be done with a one line change right here: https://sourcegraph.com/github.com/conan-io/conan/-/blob/conans/client/downloaders/caching_file_downloader.py?L114-118

```
headers = {'X-Resource-Original-Url': urls}
self._file_downloader.download(backup_url + sha256, cached_path, sha256=sha256, headers=headers)
```

My use case is that my company prevents access to the public internet by default except for specifically permitted services. If we pass this header, then all downloads can go through a service that acts as a proxy.

I've created a service that acts as a source caching proxy. When a request is made to myservice.com/<somesha>, first I check if that sha has already been downloaded, and if it has return that file immediately. If it hasn't been downloaded yet, then it reads the headers for the original URL, downloads the file, verifies it with the passed in sha, and then returns it to the client. It's an extremely simple service and this proxy means that normal users don't need to access the rest of the internet.

problem_statement.title: `primary_energy` GlobalConstraint with `investment_period` set raises `UnboundLocalError` without multi-investment periods
problem_statement.body:
> [!NOTE]
> The following content was generated by AI.

## Version Checks

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the current [`master`](https://github.com/pypsa/pypsa/tree/master) branch of PyPSA.
- [x] Also checked on the `fix/stochastic-scenario-index` branch (PR #1951), which the bug still reproduces on. This bug is independent of scenarios.

## Issue Description

In `define_primary_energy_limit` (`pypsa/optimization/global_constraints.py`),
the local variable `periods` is only assigned inside `if n._multi_invest:`
(around line 321: `periods = window.periods`). Further down, per
`GlobalConstraint`, the code does:

```python
if np.isnan(glc.investment_period):
    period_sns = sns
elif glc.investment_period in periods:
    ...
```

(`pypsa/optimization/global_constraints.py:375`, `:602` for the per-scenario
variant on the branch checked; line 375 also on `master`.)

If a `GlobalConstraint` of type `primary_energy` has `investment_period` set
(not NaN) but the network is *not* using multi-investment periods
(`n._multi_invest` is `False`, i.e. `n.snapshots` is not
`MultiIndex`-by-period), `periods` was never assigned, and the `elif` branch
raises `UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'periods'`.

A related consistency-check warning is already emitted before this
(`"The global constraints contain investment periods but snapshots are not
multi-indexed."`), but the optimization proceeds anyway and crashes with an
unrelated, confusing exception.

## Reproducible Example

```python
import pypsa

n = pypsa.Network()
n.set_snapshots(range(3))
n.add("Carrier", "gas", co2_emissions=1)
n.add("Bus", "b")
n.add("Generator", "g", bus="b", p_nom=100, marginal_cost=1, carrier="gas")
n.add("Load", "l", bus="b", p_set=50)
n.add(
    "GlobalConstraint",
    "co2_limit",
    type="primary_energy",
    carrier_attribute="co2_emissions",
    sense="<=",
    constant=100,
    investment_period=0,
)

n.optimize()
```

Traceback (identical on current `master` and on the PR #1951 branch):

```
WARNING:pypsa.consistency:The global constraints contain investment periods but snapshots are not multi-indexed.
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../pypsa/optimization/optimize.py", line 924, in create_model
    define_primary_energy_limit(n, sns, piecewise_opts)
  File ".../pypsa/optimization/global_constraints.py", line 375, in define_primary_energy_limit
    elif glc.investment_period in periods:
                                  ^^^^^^^
UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'periods' where it is not associated with a value
```

## Expected Behavior

Either:
- Raise a clear `ValueError` during consistency checking (upgrading the
  existing warning to an error) when a `GlobalConstraint` has
  `investment_period` set but the network has no multi-investment-period
  snapshots, or
- Treat the network as having a single implicit period and apply the
  constraint to all snapshots, ignoring the (irrelevant) `investment_period`
  value.

Either way, `n.optimize()` should not crash with an `UnboundLocalError` that
gives the user no indication of what is actually wrong.

## Installed Versions

<details>

pypsa 1.3.0.post1.dev20+g1052841d6 (also reproduced on master 1.3.0.post1.dev23+g02bdcbbaf)
linopy 0.9.1
pandas 3.0.3
xarray 2026.7.0

</details>

title: Fix NegativeBinomialLikelihood parameter order for multivariate series
issue_title: [BUG] NegativeBinomialLikelihood: wrong parameter order for multivariate series, and mu is not the mean

install_config.install: pip install -e . --quiet && pip install pytest pytest-cov pytest-timeout testfixtures --quiet

gold_patch:
diff --git a/CHANGELOG.md b/CHANGELOG.md
index 9d0bf18770..401d7d45e4 100644
--- a/CHANGELOG.md
+++ b/CHANGELOG.md
@@ -15,6 +15,8 @@ but cannot always guarantee backwards compatibility. Changes that may **break co
 
 - Fixed safe-loading for multi-output `SKLearnModel` where Darts' `MultiOutputMixin` was not recognized as a safe-global. [#3261](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3261) by [Miral Amin](https://github.com/aminmiral).
 - Fixed `ForecastingModel.backtest()` ignoring `val_length` when no `historical_forecasts` are passed. [#3204](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3204) by [Dennis Bader](https://github.com/dennisbader) and [#3264](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3264) by [Nathan Chandrasekar](https://github.com/vera-rubin).
+- Fixed `NegativeBinomialLikelihood` returning the distribution parameters in the wrong order with `predict_likelihood_parameters=True` on multivariate series; parameters are now grouped by component, as with all other likelihood models. [#3243](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3243) by [Abhay Juloori](https://github.com/AbhayJuloori).
+- 🔴 Fixed `NegativeBinomialLikelihood` mapping the network outputs to a distribution whose mean was not the predicted mean `mu`. The model now outputs the mean `mu` and dispersion `alpha` (variance `mu + alpha * mu**2`) as intended. Models trained with this likelihood in earlier versions will produce different forecasts and should be retrained. [#3243](https://github.com/unit8co/darts/pull/3243) by [Abhay Juloori](https://github.com/AbhayJuloori).
 
 **Dependencies**
 
diff --git a/darts/utils/likelihood_models/torch.py b/darts/utils/likelihood_models/torch.py
index d4a1b16cb3..c180fb380d 100644
--- a/darts/utils/likelihood_models/torch.py
+++ b/darts/utils/likelihood_models/torch.py
@@ -398,8 +398,10 @@ def __init__(self):
         - Support: :math:`\\mathbb{N}_0` (natural numbers including 0).
         - Parameters: number of failures :math:`r > 0`, success probability :math:`p \\in (0, 1)`.
 
-        Behind the scenes the distribution is reparameterized so that the actual outputs of the
-        network are in terms of the mean :math:`\\mu` and shape :math:`\\alpha`.
+        Behind the scenes the network outputs the mean :math:`\\mu > 0` and the dispersion :math:`\\alpha > 0`
+        (variance :math:`\\mu + \\alpha \\mu^2`), which are mapped to :math:`r = 1 / \\alpha` and
+        :math:`p = \\mu / (\\mu + r)`. The returned :math:`p` follows PyTorch's convention (mean
+        :math:`r p / (1 - p)`).
         """
         self.softplus = nn.Softplus()
         super().__init__(
@@ -413,30 +415,39 @@ def _prior_params(self) -> tuple[Any, ...] | None:
         return None
 
     @staticmethod
-    def _get_r_and_p_from_mu_and_alpha(mu, alpha):
-        # See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_binomial_distribution for the different parametrizations
+    def _get_r_and_logits_from_mu_and_alpha(
+        mu: torch.Tensor, alpha: torch.Tensor
+    ) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
+        # See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_binomial_distribution for the different parametrizations.
+        # With r = 1 / alpha, the mean r * p / (1 - p) equals mu for p = mu / (mu + r), i.e.
+        # logits = log(p / (1 - p)) = log(mu * alpha). Using logits keeps the log-likelihood stable when p -> 1.

problem_statement.title: [BUG] NegativeBinomialLikelihood: wrong parameter order for multivariate series, and mu is not the mean
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**
Two things in `NegativeBinomialLikelihood`:

1. `predict_likelihood_parameters()` returns the parameters in the wrong order for multivariate series. It does `torch.cat([r, p], dim=-1)`, so the output is `r_a, r_b, p_a, p_b`, but the component names are `a_r, a_p, b_r, b_p` (grouped per component, like the base `TorchLikelihood` does). So with `predict(..., predict_likelihood_parameters=True)` the values end up under the wrong names, e.g. `a_p` contains `b`'s `r`.

2. The docstring says the network outputs the mean `mu` and shape `alpha`, but `mu` isn't the mean of the resulting distribution. `p` is computed as `r / (mu + r)`, which is the success probability in the Wikipedia parametrization (mean `r(1-p)/p`), but torch's `NegativeBinomial(total_count, probs)` has mean `r * p / (1 - p)`. So the actual mean is `r**2 / mu`. Training still works since the mapping is a bijection, but `mu` doesn't mean what the docs say.

**To Reproduce**
```python
import torch
from darts.utils.likelihood_models import NegativeBinomialLikelihood

lkl = NegativeBinomialLikelihood()
# raw model output: (n_samples, n_timesteps, n_components, n_params)
out = torch.tensor([[[[1.0, 2.0], [10.0, 20.0]]]])

names = lkl.component_names(components=["a", "b"])
params = lkl.predict_likelihood_parameters(out)[0, 0]
r_a, p_a = lkl.predict_likelihood_parameters(out[:, :, :1])[0, 0]
r_b, p_b = lkl.predict_likelihood_parameters(out[:, :, 1:])[0, 0]
print(dict(zip(names, params.tolist())))
print(f"a alone: r={r_a:.4f}, p={p_a:.4f} | b alone: r={r_b:.4f}, p={p_b:.4f}")

mu, alpha = lkl._params_from_output(out)
print("mu:", mu.flatten().tolist())
print("mean:", lkl._distr_from_params((mu, alpha)).mean.flatten().tolist())
```
Output:
```
{'a_r': 0.4702, 'a_p': 0.0500, 'b_r': 0.2636, 'b_p': 0.0050}
a alone: r=0.4702, p=0.2636 | b alone: r=0.0500, p=0.0050
mu: [1.3133, 10.0000]
mean: [0.1683, 0.0002]
```

**Expected behavior**
1. `a_r, a_p, b_r, b_p` should be `0.4702, 0.2636, 0.0500, 0.0050`.
2. The distribution mean should equal `mu` (i.e. `p = mu / (mu + r)` with torch's convention).

**System (please complete the following information):**
 - Python version: 3.13
 - darts version: 0.47.0 (also on current master)

**Additional context**
I checked the other univariate torch likelihoods the same way (multivariate output vs. per-component outputs) and only NB is affected; the others use the base class interleaving. The existing multivariate test only checks the component names, not the values, which is probably why this slipped through.

Happy to open a PR. For 1 it's a small fix plus a test. For 2, changing `p` to `mu / (mu + r)` would change what previously trained models output after loading, so I wanted to check first: would you prefer fixing the parametrization, or keeping it and just correcting the docstring?

As of today there is no option in Briefcase when building Windows MSI installers to customize the final page of the installer (the page shown when setup finishes). problem_statement.title: _is_wheel_built() raises fatal ValueError for pre-built packages with build tags after #1273
problem_statement.body:
After #1273, `_is_wheel_built()` crashes with a `ValueError` when a candidate wheel on a package index carries a build tag but the local configuration expects none.

```
ValueError: torch: changelog for version 2.11.0 is inconsistent.
Found build tag (2, '') but expected (0, '')
```

Pre-built packages return an empty build tag from `PackageBuildInfo.build_tag()` ([`_pbi.py:298-300`](https://github.com/python-wheel-build/fromager/blob/1d07f3088f7c365ecbc0bec229c3beb7086ebcf0/src/fromager/packagesettings/_pbi.py#L298-L300)) because we assume pre-built wheels come from PyPI and do not have a fromager build tag. When a separate package index (configured via `wheel_server_url`) hosts a wheel with a build tag > 0, the consistency check at [`build.py:548-554`](https://github.com/python-wheel-build/fromager/blob/1e3c39d7/src/fromager/commands/build.py#L548-L554) raises.

This check existed before #1273 but was inside the broad `try/except Exception` block that caught it and treated it as a cache miss (`return None`). The refactoring in #1273 moved the candidate iteration loop outside that exception handler, making the previously-swallowed `ValueError` fatal.

## How to reproduce

1. Configure a package as `pre_built` with a `wheel_server_url` pointing to a package index (e.g. torch with a GitLab PyPI registry)
2. Ensure that index has a wheel with a build tag > 0 (e.g. `torch-2.11.0-2-cp312-cp312-linux_aarch64.whl`)
3. Run a build that looks up that package:
   ```
   fromager build torch==2.11.0
   ```
4. The build fails with:
   ```
   ValueError: torch: changelog for version 2.11.0 is inconsistent. Found build tag (2, '') but expected (0, '')
   ```

**Expected behavior:** The build tag mismatch should be treated as a cache miss (log and skip the candidate), matching the pre-#1273 behavior.

+
+# About this test: _LuatexKpsewhich.search() communicates with a long-lived `luatex`
+# subprocess over pipes and turns whatever comes back into one of three
+# outcomes that its caller (find_tex_file) depends on:
+#   * a path string  -> luatex found the file;
+#   * ""             -> luatex works but the file genuinely doesn't exist;
+#   * None           -> luatex is unusable, so the caller must fall back to
+#                       running kpsewhich directly.
+# Each parametrized case below feeds search() one scenario and asserts it maps
+# to the right outcome.
+#
+# Notice: We use mock-based testing here for cross-platform compatibility and
+# deterministic/standardized testing. This means that testing is quite heavily
+# tied to the internals of the tested function. Restructuring or rewriting of
+# code might break testing without actually changing the overall behaviour.
+# This tradeoff was accepted in #31984.
+@pytest.mark.parametrize("readline, write_error, expected", [
+    # (bytes luatex "prints", exception raised on write, expected return)
+    # Case 1: supply a path with no error; check search() passes it through
+    (b"/texmf/pdftex.map\n", None, "/texmf/pdftex.map"),
+    # Case 2: make luatex answer "nil" (file missing); check search() returns ""
+    (b"nil\n", None, ""),
+    # Case 3: supply an empty read (luatex died); check search() returns None
+    (b"", None, None),
+    # Case 4: raise an error on write (pipe broke); check search() returns None
+    (b"unused", BrokenPipeError, None),
+])
+def test_luatexkpsewhich_search(readline, write_error, expected):
+    proc = mock.Mock()  # stand-in for the luatex subprocess
+    proc.poll.return_value = None  # so search() won't mark it dead and restart it
+    proc.stdin.write.side_effect = write_error  # None => write ok; else pipe broke
+    proc.stdout.readline.return_value = readline  # luatex's answer, read by search()
+    lk = object.__new__(dr._LuatexKpsewhich)  # bypass __new__ (spawns a real luatex)
+    lk._proc = proc  # hand search() our fake process instead
+    assert lk.search("pdftex.map") == expected
+
+
+def test_find_tex_file_fallback_to_kpsewhich(monkeypatch):
+    # Unlike the search() test above, this checks the routing in find_tex_file,
+    # which takes the result of search() and acts accordingly by either calling
+    # the fallback (kpsewhich) if the search failed via luatex, or just forwarding
+    # the results. We therefore replace the whole _LuatexKpsewhich with a stub
+    # whose search() always returns None (luatex unusable), and check that
+    # find_tex_file then falls back to kpsewhich.
+    class _UnusableLuatex:

+    # kpsewhich is run via cbook._check_and_log_subprocess; intercept it so no

+    commands = []

problem_statement.title: BUG: pm.fit(..., backend="jax") fails for every model: ADVI approximation parameters lack static shapes
problem_statement.body:
### Describe the issue:

The `backend` argument added to `fit` in #679ff1235 ("Add backend argument to all methods") does not work with `backend="jax"` for variational inference — for any model. Compiling the ADVI step function with the JAX linker fails while tracing.

Root cause: `MeanFieldGroup.create_shared_params` creates the approximation parameters without static shapes (`pymc/variational/approximations.py`, `"mu"`/`"rho"`), so they enter the graph as `TensorType(float64, shape=(?,))` even though `self.ddim` is known at creation time. Broadcasting the `(1, ddim)` Monte-Carlo noise against the `(1, ?)` entropy term forces a runtime-shape `Alloc`, and the JAX backend cannot trace shapes that are traced values. The `JAXLinker` static-input machinery (`scalar_shape_inputs`) does not apply because the offending shape scalar is computed inside the graph, not a direct input feeding only `JAXShapeTuple` nodes.

Reproduced on 6.1.0 and current `main` (`9d242603d`). Patching `create_shared_params` to pass `shape=(self.ddim,)` to `pytensor.shared` for `mu` and `rho` makes the reproducer below pass; `FullRankGroup` (`mu`, `L_tril`) and `EmpiricalGroup` (`histogram`) have the same problem.

I have a validated fix branch ready to submit as a PR. Note it needs one companion change beyond the `create_shared_params` shapes: with statically-shaped parameters, `Group._initial_type` must also carry `shape=(None, self.ddim)` (and `symbolic_initial` must be created after `self.ordering` is populated), otherwise `ddim == 1` models fail with a scan broadcast-pattern inconsistency (`test_elbo`, `test_elbo_beta_kl`, `test_scale_cost_to_minibatch_works` in the existing suite). With both changes the full `tests/variational/` suite passes (330 passed, 10 skipped).

### Reproduceable code example:

```python
import numpy as np
import pymc as pm

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
y = rng.normal(size=20)

with pm.Model():
    mu = pm.Normal("mu", 0, 1)
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", 1)
    pm.Normal("y", mu, sigma, observed=y)
    approx = pm.fit(n=1, method="advi", backend="jax", progressbar=False)
```

### Error message:

```shell
<details>

  File ".../pytensor/link/jax/dispatch/tensor_basic.py", line 46, in alloc
    res = jnp.broadcast_to(x, shape)
  ...
  File ".../jax/_src/core.py", line 2135, in canonicalize_shape
    raise _invalid_shape_error(shape, context)
TypeError: Shapes must be 1D sequences of concrete values of integer type, got (JitTracer(int64[]),).
If using `jit`, try using `static_argnums` or applying `jit` to smaller subfunctions.
The error occurred while tracing the function jax_funcified_fgraph at ... for jit.

(with exception_verbosity=high, the failing node is
 `alloc(tensor_constant, tensor_variable)` in the ELBO entropy term, downstream of
 `Log(ExpandDims(Softplus(rho)))` where rho: Vector(float64, shape=(?,)))

</details>
```

### PyMC version information:

```
PyMC version: 6.1.0 (also reproduced on main @ 9d242603d)
PyTensor version: 3.1.3
JAX version: 0.10.2
Python version: 3.14.6
Operating system: macOS (Apple Silicon, CPU-only JAX)
How did you install PyMC: pip (via uv)
```

### Context for the issue:

This blocks GPU-backed VI for downstream libraries wrapping expensive likelihoods — concretely HSSM's neural-network (LAN) likelihoods (lnccbrown/HSSM#1056, fixed downstream in lnccbrown/HSSM#1059 with a temporary scoped workaround that re-creates the shared parameters with static shapes; it self-disables once this is fixed upstream). Note that even with this fixed, `approx.sample()` after a JAX-backend fit fails separately because the JAX-compiled step function leaves `jax.Array` objects in shared-variable storage, which the default numba-compiled sampling function cannot type — filed separately (see linked issue in first comment).
